question: What is the difference between composition and inheritance?
title: Composition vs Inheritance — has-a vs is-a
direct_answer: Inheritance is an is-a relationship where a subclass extends a parent class and inherits all its methods and state, like Dog extends Animal. Composition is a has-a relationship where a class contains instances of other classes as fields, like Car has an Engine. Inheritance is decided at compile time and cannot change, while composition allows swapping out collaborators at runtime.

sections.title: Two Fundamentally Different Mechanisms for Code Reuse
sections.content: **Inheritance** and **composition** are both ways to reuse code, but they create very different relationships. Inheritance models an **is-a** relationship: when Dog extends Animal, we're saying a Dog IS-A kind of Animal. The subclass inherits all fields, methods, and behavior from the parent. **Composition** models a **has-a** relationship: a Car HAS-A Engine, implemented by holding an Engine field. The Car uses the Engine by calling methods on it, but doesn't become an Engine. Think of inheritance as a blueprint hierarchy (fixed at compile time) and composition as LEGO bricks (you can swap pieces at runtime). Modern design principles strongly favor composition because it keeps classes decoupled and testable. When you inherit, you're locked into the parent's implementation details; when you compose, you depend only on an interface contract.

sections.title: When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content: **Use inheritance when** you have a true taxonomic is-a relationship where the subclass is genuinely a specialized version of the parent and will use most of its behavior. For example, a SavingsAccount extending BankAccount makes sense because every savings account truly is a bank account. **Use composition when** you need flexibility, testability, or when the relationship is more about using behavior than being a kind of something. For example, a NotificationService that has-a EmailSender and has-a SMSSender allows you to inject different implementations in tests and swap them based on configuration. The default choice in modern Java should be composition unless you have a compelling reason for inheritance. Ask yourself: does this class need to be treated polymorphically as the parent type, or does it just need some of the parent's functionality?

sections.title: Key Points
content: **is-a vs has-a**: Inheritance models type hierarchies (Dog is an Animal), composition models collaboration (Car has an Engine).
**Compile-time vs runtime**: Inheritance locks you in at compile time; composition lets you swap collaborators dynamically.
**Coupling**: Inheritance creates tight coupling to parent internals; composition depends only on interface contracts.
**Fragile base class**: Changes to a parent class can break subclasses unexpectedly, a risk composition avoids.
**Gang of Four principle**: Favor composition over inheritance is the default stance in object-oriented design.
**Testing**: Composition makes testing easier because you can inject mock collaborators; inheritance requires setting up parent state.
**Real-world Spring**: Spring dependency injection is built on composition, injecting collaborators into fields rather than using inheritance chains.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Inheritance and composition are two ways to reuse code in Java, but they create very different relationships. Inheritance is an is-a relationship where a subclass extends a parent and inherits all its behavior. For example, if Dog extends Animal, a Dog is a kind of Animal and gets all Animal methods. Composition is a has-a relationship where one class holds another as a field. A Car has an Engine, so the Car class contains an Engine field and uses it by delegation. The key difference is flexibility. Inheritance is decided at compile time and you can't change it, so if Dog extends Animal, that's fixed. With composition, you can swap out the Engine at runtime by injecting a different implementation. Composition also creates looser coupling because the Car only depends on the Engine interface, not its internal implementation. The Gang of Four design patterns book famously says favor composition over inheritance, and that's the default approach in modern Java. One common pitfall freshers fall into is thinking inheritance saves more code, so it must be better. But inheritance couples you tightly to the parent class, making changes risky. If the parent class changes its internals, all subclasses can break, that's called the fragile base class problem. In a Spring Boot app, you'll see composition everywhere. Services have repository fields injected, controllers have service fields injected, and we rarely use deep inheritance hierarchies. That makes the code flexible and easy to test because you can inject mocks. So to sum up, inheritance is for true is-a relationships where polymorphism matters, but composition is the safer default for code reuse.

title: Favor composition over inheritance — why?
direct_answer: Composition is preferred because it creates loose coupling, allows runtime flexibility, and makes testing easier. When you use composition, a class depends on an interface contract, not on the internal implementation of a parent class. You can inject different collaborators at runtime and swap them in tests with mocks. Inheritance creates tight coupling because subclasses depend on parent internals, leading to the fragile base class problem where parent changes can unexpectedly break subclasses.

sections.title: Why the Default Should Be Composition
sections.content: The Gang of Four design patterns book established **favor composition over inheritance** as a core principle, and decades of production Java have proven it right. Composition wins on three dimensions: **flexibility**, **coupling**, and **testability**. When you compose objects, you depend on their public interface contracts, not their implementation details. That means you can swap collaborators at runtime based on configuration or inject mocks during testing. Inheritance, by contrast, locks you into the parent class at compile time and exposes you to its internal behavior. Even a seemingly harmless refactor in the parent can ripple through and break subclasses in unexpected ways, a phenomenon known as the **fragile base class problem**. In modern Spring Boot applications, you'll rarely see deep inheritance hierarchies. Instead, services hold repositories as fields, controllers hold services as fields, all wired through dependency injection, which is fundamentally composition-based.

sections.title: Composition Provides Flexibility and Testability
Key Points
content: **Loose coupling**: Composition depends on interface contracts, not concrete parent implementations, reducing ripple effects from changes.
**Runtime flexibility**: You can inject different collaborators based on environment or configuration without recompiling.
**Easier testing**: Inject mock or stub implementations during tests instead of setting up complex parent class state.
**Fragile base class problem**: Inheritance exposes subclasses to parent internals, so parent refactors can break subclasses unpredictably.
**Encapsulation violation**: Inheritance leaks parent implementation details to subclasses, breaking the black-box principle.
**Spring DI philosophy**: Spring's dependency injection is built on composition, injecting collaborators into fields rather than extending base classes.
**Single Responsibility Principle**: Composition supports SRP by letting each class do one thing and delegate the rest, rather than inheriting a grab-bag of parent behavior.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Composition is preferred over inheritance because it gives you flexibility, loose coupling, and easier testing. When you use composition, your class holds collaborators as fields and depends only on their interface contracts, not their internal implementation. That means you can swap out those collaborators at runtime. For example, in production your NotificationService might use an EmailSender, but in tests you can inject a mock that doesn't actually send emails. You can't do that with inheritance because the parent class is baked in at compile time. Inheritance also creates tight coupling because the subclass depends on the parent's internals. If the parent class changes how it implements something, even if it's just a refactor, that can break subclasses in unexpected ways. That's called the fragile base class problem. It's a real risk in production code. Another issue is that inheritance violates encapsulation. When you extend a class, you're exposed to its private and protected fields and methods. You're no longer treating it as a black box, you're reaching into its guts. That makes the code fragile over time. In a Spring Boot app, you'll see composition everywhere. Services have repositories injected, controllers have services injected, all through dependency injection. We rarely use deep inheritance hierarchies anymore. The Gang of Four design patterns book said favor composition over inheritance back in the nineties, and that's still the default rule today. One mistake freshers make is thinking inheritance saves more code because you get everything from the parent for free. But that free code comes with hidden costs in coupling and fragility. Composition is more explicit, you have to write delegation code, but it's also safer and more maintainable in the long run.

question: What is the fragile base class problem?
title: Fragile base class problem in Java inheritance
direct_answer: The fragile base class problem occurs when a seemingly safe change to a parent class breaks one or more subclasses, even though the parent change appeared correct. Because subclasses depend on the parent's internal implementation details, not just its public interface, any refactor to the parent can have unexpected ripple effects on inherited or overridden behavior in subclasses. This makes maintenance risky because you can't safely evolve the parent class without auditing every subclass.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of a specific, named pitfall of inheritance that explains why composition is safer.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not being familiar with the term or thinking it's just about breaking the public API, when it's actually about implementation coupling.

sections.title: When a Parent Class Change Breaks Its Children
sections.content: The **fragile base class problem** is a well-known hazard of inheritance where changes to a parent class, even internal refactors that seem safe, break subclasses in subtle and unexpected ways. The root cause is that subclasses depend not just on the parent's public interface, but on its **internal implementation details** and the way methods call each other. When a subclass overrides a method, it's making assumptions about how the parent's other methods work. If the parent refactors its internals and changes those call patterns, the subclass behavior can break without any warning from the compiler. This is why inheritance is often described as **white-box reuse** (you must know the parent's internals) versus composition's **black-box reuse** (you depend only on the public contract). The fragile base class problem is a major reason why modern design favors composition and why frameworks like Spring rarely use deep inheritance hierarchies.

sections.title: A Parent Refactor That Breaks a Subclass
Key Points
content: **Internal coupling**: Subclasses depend on parent's internal implementation, not just its public API, creating hidden dependencies.
**Overriding risks**: When a subclass overrides a method, it assumes the parent's other methods will call it in a certain way.
**Refactor brittleness**: Safe-looking parent refactors can break subclass behavior without any compile-time warning.
**White-box reuse**: Inheritance requires knowing parent internals (white-box), unlike composition's black-box approach.
**Maintenance burden**: You can't safely evolve a parent class without auditing every subclass that depends on it.
**Composition avoids it**: Composed objects interact only through public interfaces, so internal refactors don't break clients.
**Joshua Bloch's advice**: Effective Java says design and document for inheritance or prohibit it, highlighting the risk.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The fragile base class problem happens when you change a parent class and it breaks subclasses, even though the change to the parent seemed totally safe. The problem is that subclasses don't just depend on the parent's public methods, they depend on how those methods are implemented internally and how they call each other. Let me give you a concrete example. Say you have a Counter class with an add method and an addAll method. The addAll method internally calls add for each value in the list. Now imagine a subclass called InstrumentedCounter that overrides add to count how many times it's called. It works fine at first. But then someone refactors the parent's addAll method to be more efficient by using a stream and summing the values directly, without calling add anymore. Suddenly the InstrumentedCounter breaks because it's no longer counting those calls, but the compiler doesn't warn you. That's the fragile base class problem. The parent change was correct and improved performance, but it broke the subclass because the subclass was relying on internal behavior, not just the public contract. This is why inheritance is called white-box reuse. You have to know the parent's internals to safely extend it. Composition avoids this problem entirely because composed objects interact only through public interfaces. If a collaborator refactors its internal implementation, it doesn't affect the client as long as the public contract stays the same. Joshua Bloch's Effective Java book says you should either design and document a class specifically for inheritance, or prohibit inheritance entirely by making the class final. The fragile base class problem is a big reason why modern Java code favors composition over inheritance for flexibility and safety.

question: When is inheritance the right choice over composition?
title: When to use inheritance — valid use cases
direct_answer: Inheritance is the right choice when there's a true is-a relationship where the subclass genuinely is a specialized version of the parent, and you need polymorphism to treat different subclasses uniformly through the parent interface. It's appropriate when the subclass will use most of the parent's behavior and only differs in specific details. The litmus test is whether the subclass is a kind of the parent in a real-world sense, not just borrowing some behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can show balance and nuance, defending inheritance when it's genuinely appropriate rather than dogmatically rejecting it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying composition is always better without recognizing legitimate use cases for inheritance, which makes you sound inexperienced.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between taxonomic is-a relationships (inheritance appropriate) and behavioral is-a relationships (composition often better).

sections.title: Recognizing When Inheritance Is the Better Tool
sections.content: While the principle is **favor composition over inheritance**, favor doesn't mean always. Inheritance has legitimate uses, and knowing when to apply it shows design maturity. Inheritance makes sense when you have a **true taxonomic is-a relationship** where the subclass is genuinely a kind of the parent in the domain model. A SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount, a Manager IS-A Employee, a Rectangle IS-A Shape. The key is that the relationship must be meaningful in the problem domain, not just a way to reuse code. Inheritance also shines when you need **polymorphism** to treat different subclasses uniformly through a common parent interface, like a list of Shapes where you call draw on each one and the correct subclass implementation runs. The decision comes down to asking: does this subclass need to be treated as an instance of the parent type, or does it just need some of the parent's functionality?

sections.title: Step 1: Verify the Is-A Relationship Is Taxonomic, Not Just Behavioral
sections.content: The first test is whether the is-a relationship is **taxonomic** (about what the thing is) versus **behavioral** (about what the thing does). A Dog is-a Animal is taxonomic because in the real world, a dog truly is a kind of animal. But if you're tempted to make a Car extend Engine because Car has-a Engine and uses its behavior, that's a behavioral is-a, which is wrong. Ask yourself: in plain English, does it make sense to say the subclass is a kind of the parent? If someone on the business side heard you say a Manager is a kind of Employee, would they nod in agreement? If the is-a feels forced or exists only to reuse code, it's a smell that composition is better. Another check is the **Liskov Substitution Principle**: can you pass a subclass instance anywhere the parent is expected without breaking behavior? If not, the is-a relationship is broken and you shouldn't use inheritance.

sections.title: Step 2: Confirm Polymorphism Is Actually Needed
sections.content: Inheritance makes sense when you need to treat different subclasses uniformly through the parent type, a capability called **polymorphism**. For example, if you have a list of Shapes and you want to call draw on each one, letting each subclass (Circle, Rectangle, Triangle) provide its own implementation, inheritance is the right tool. The alternative with composition would require a lot of type-checking and casting, which defeats the purpose of polymorphism. However, if you don't need to treat objects uniformly, if you're just reusing some parent behavior in isolation, then inheritance is overkill and composition is cleaner. A good test is whether you'll ever store subclass instances in a collection typed as the parent or pass them to methods that accept the parent type. If the answer is no, you probably don't need inheritance. In Spring Boot, you'll see inheritance used for things like custom exception hierarchies (CustomBusinessException extends RuntimeException) where you want to catch all custom exceptions polymorphically.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Taxonomic is-a**: Inheritance is appropriate when the subclass is genuinely a kind of the parent in the domain model, like Dog is-a Animal.
**Polymorphism need**: Use inheritance when you need to treat different subclasses uniformly through the parent type, calling overridden methods.
**Liskov Substitution Principle**: The subclass must be substitutable for the parent without breaking expectations or behavior.
**Avoid behavioral is-a**: Don't use inheritance just to reuse behavior; that's composition's job (Car has-a Engine, not is-a Engine).
**Template Method pattern**: Inheritance is appropriate when the parent defines an algorithm skeleton and subclasses fill in specific steps.
**Spring exception hierarchies**: Custom exceptions often extend RuntimeException to enable polymorphic catch blocks.
**Design for inheritance**: If you use inheritance, document the contract and make it explicit which methods are meant to be overridden.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Inheritance is the right choice when you have a true is-a relationship and you need polymorphism. The key word is true. The relationship has to make sense in the real world, not just in code. If someone on the business side would agree that a SavingsAccount is a kind of BankAccount, that's a good sign inheritance fits. But if you're only using inheritance to reuse some code, that's a smell that composition is better. The first step is to check if the is-a relationship is taxonomic or just behavioral. Taxonomic means it's about what the thing is. A Manager is an Employee, that's taxonomic. But if you're tempted to make a Car extend Engine just because Car uses Engine behavior, that's behavioral and you should use composition instead. The second step is to confirm you actually need polymorphism. Polymorphism is when you treat different subclasses uniformly through the parent type. For example, you have a list of Shapes and you call draw on each one, and each subclass, Circle, Rectangle, Triangle, provides its own implementation. That's a perfect use case for inheritance. Without it, you'd be stuck with type-checking and casting, which defeats the purpose. In a Spring Boot app, you'll see inheritance used for things like custom exception hierarchies. You might have a CustomBusinessException that extends RuntimeException, and then specific exceptions like OrderNotFoundException or PaymentFailedException that extend CustomBusinessException. That lets you catch all custom exceptions polymorphically in a global exception handler. One mistake freshers make is saying composition is always better, which sounds dogmatic. Interviewers want to see nuance. You should be able to defend inheritance when it's appropriate. Another pitfall is using inheritance just to reuse code without a real is-a relationship. That creates fragile designs. So to sum up, use inheritance when the subclass truly is a kind of the parent and you need polymorphism to treat subclasses uniformly. Otherwise, favor composition for flexibility and safety.

question: How does the Decorator pattern use composition instead of inheritance?
title: Decorator pattern — composition to extend behavior at runtime
direct_answer: The Decorator pattern uses composition to add behavior to an object dynamically without subclassing. A decorator wraps the original object by holding it as a field that implements the same interface. The decorator implements the same interface, delegates to the wrapped object, and adds extra behavior before or after delegation. This allows combining features at runtime without the class explosion that would result from creating a subclass for every combination of features.

sections.title: Dynamically Adding Behavior Through Wrapping
sections.content: The **Decorator pattern** is a textbook example of **composition over inheritance** in action. Instead of creating subclasses to add new behavior, you wrap an object in a decorator that implements the same interface. The decorator holds the original object as a field and **delegates** method calls to it, adding extra behavior before or after the delegation. This means you can stack decorators at runtime to combine features without creating a combinatorial explosion of subclasses. For example, imagine you have a DataSource interface with a read method. You could create decorators like EncryptedDataSource, CompressedDataSource, and CachedDataSource. Each one wraps a DataSource and adds one feature. You can then combine them at runtime: new CachedDataSource(new EncryptedDataSource(new CompressedDataSource(fileDataSource))). With inheritance, you'd need a separate subclass for every combination, leading to dozens of classes. Java's I/O streams are a classic real-world example: BufferedReader wraps FileReader, which wraps an underlying stream, each adding buffering or character decoding.

sections.title: Decorator Pattern in Action
Key Points
content: **Same interface**: Decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, making it transparent to clients.
**Composition over inheritance**: Uses a has-a relationship (holds wrapped object as field) instead of extends.
**Runtime flexibility**: You can combine decorators in any order at runtime without creating new classes for each combination.
**Single Responsibility**: Each decorator adds one feature, keeping classes focused and following SRP.
**Java I/O example**: BufferedReader wraps FileReader wraps FileInputStream, each adding a layer of functionality.
**Spring proxies**: Spring uses decoration for transaction management and AOP, wrapping beans in proxies that add behavior.
**Avoids class explosion**: Without Decorator, you'd need a subclass for every feature combination (MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, etc.).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Decorator pattern uses composition instead of inheritance to add behavior to objects dynamically. Instead of creating a subclass for each new feature, you wrap the original object in a decorator that implements the same interface. The decorator holds the wrapped object as a field and delegates method calls to it, adding extra behavior before or after the delegation. Let me give you a concrete example. Say you have a Coffee interface with methods like getDescription and getCost. You start with a SimpleCoffee implementation. Now you want to add features like milk and sugar. With inheritance, you'd create subclasses like MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, and MilkSugarCoffee. But that explodes quickly if you have many features because you need a subclass for every combination. With the Decorator pattern, you create a MilkDecorator and a SugarDecorator. Each one wraps a Coffee object and implements the Coffee interface. The MilkDecorator's getCost method calls the wrapped coffee's getCost and adds the milk cost. Then you can stack them at runtime like new SugarDecorator wrapping new MilkDecorator wrapping new SimpleCoffee. You get all the features combined without creating a single new class for that combination. A real-world Java example is BufferedReader wrapping FileReader. BufferedReader adds buffering behavior by holding a FileReader as a field and delegating read calls to it. It doesn't extend FileReader, it wraps it. That's composition. In Spring, you'll see decoration used for transaction management. When you put the at-Transactional annotation on a method, Spring wraps your bean in a proxy that adds transaction behavior before and after your method runs. One mistake freshers make is thinking Decorator is about inheritance because the base decorator class might extend something. But the key is that it holds the wrapped object as a field, that's composition. The extension is just to share code between concrete decorators. So to sum up, the Decorator pattern shows how composition gives you runtime flexibility to combine behaviors without the class explosion you'd get from inheritance.
